problems.description: Deletes the entire existing 200-line seed codebase (index.ts, a JWT auth API) and replaces it with an unrelated flat-file static site generator (package name changes to flat-file-ssg). This is an off-domain rewrite that discards all prior functionality, breaks any consumers/tests of the exported Express `app`, and abandons the existing project structure.

package.json dependency set is swapped wholesale (jsonwebtoken/bcryptjs/better-sqlite3 removed for commander/gray-matter/marked), so existing test and runtime surface of the auth API is silently invalidated rather than incrementally evolved.

44 convention violations introduced in new code (cli.ts, config.ts, core.ts): classes/interfaces not PascalCase, constants not UPPER_CASE, snake_case function names — directly contradicting the PascalCase style of the code it replaced.
Convention score of 0.49 with 44 violations sits well below the standard the existing index.ts demonstrated (PascalCase interfaces/classes), so the new code regresses style consistency.

strengths: New code is modular (split across cli.ts, config.ts, core.ts, index.ts) rather than a 200-line monolith.
Mechanical measurements show no new bugs, no new duplications, and -5 SonarQube smells.
package.json is well-formed with build/test scripts, bin entry, files allowlist, and Node engines constraint.
commit_reviews.summary: A greenfield session that went off-task architecturally — it deleted the working auth API and replaced it with an unrelated static site generator, but improved modularity and static-analysis health along the way.

The measured score is ground truth, though the truncated diff means pre-existing vs new violations can't be fully separated.

problems.description: config.ts loadTypeScriptModule monkey-patches require.extensions['.ts'] to load TypeScript configs, mutating global module-resolution state (restored in finally, but fragile, CJS-only, and won't compose with ESM). Prefer a real loader (tsx/ts-node/esbuild) or support JS/JSON configs.
Bundling 'typescript' as a runtime config transpiler is a heavyweight dependency for what could be handled at config-load time or with a lighter loader.

core.ts createBuildEngine closure carries three mutable state flags plus a nested run() hook dispatcher, contributing +33 cognitive complexity per SonarQube; hook dispatch could be extracted into a small runner.

Static analysis flags snake_case in config.ts and naming violations across cli.ts/config.ts/core.ts (44 total, score 0.49); the visible PascalCase complaints look like analyzer misparses of already-correct names, but the snake_case and constant-naming ones are plausibly real.
config.ts reads the file via require('node:fs').readFileSync while the module already imports promises as fs — inconsistent I/O style.
No tests accompany the refactor of the core build path and new config loader, despite +572/-302 lines of churn (diff is truncated, so this is based on visible files).

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: config resolution, build engine, and public API split into cohesive modules
Public API preserved (buildSite/Page/BuildOptions unchanged) — backward-compatible refactor
Lifecycle guarded with started/ended/building flags preventing duplicate or re-entrant builds
Plugin hook model (onStart/beforeBuild/afterBuild/onEnd) cleanly extends the existing plugin architecture
Monolithic index.ts reduced from 227 to 14 lines via re-export
commit_reviews.summary: A directionally sound modularization that preserves the public API and plugin architecture, but the require.extensions config-loader hack and rising complexity (convention 0.49/44 flags, +33 cognitive complexity) are technical debt; the mechanical convention score appears partly inflated by analyzer false positives on already-PascalCase names, so qualitative adherence reads higher than the 0.49 measurement.

problems.description: Incremental-cache logic is embedded directly in core build() instead of implemented through the existing plugin seam (beforeBuild hooks). The codebase already defines a Plugin abstraction; hardcoding cache/clean/stats into the engine bypasses it, reducing reuse and testability for alternative backends.

Single .ssg-cache.json manifest serializes full PluginPage objects (including data) for the entire site. Read/write/parse of this file is O(site size) every build, which undermines the incremental benefit at scale; a per-file content-addressed cache would scale better. Also invalidation keys only on source+template hash, so plugin/other-input changes can serve stale pages.

build() now handles clean, incremental, manifest read/write, hashing, and stats inline; cognitive complexity +24 per SonarQube. The cache read/write and invalidation-decision logic should be decomposed into smaller helpers.
engine.end() runs in a finally block without guarding whether start()/build() actually ran; if build() throws before initialization completes, end() may execute against a half-initialized engine.
timeSavedMs is a fabricated heuristic (true 'time saved' cannot be measured without running the skipped work) and template contents are re-hashed in full on every build.

strengths: Sound incremental-build semantics: clean flag, missing-manifest full rebuild, and template-hash invalidation are all wired consistently.
cachedPage() deep-copies tags/data before reuse, avoiding aliasing mutations of cached entries.
Extends the existing BuildEngine/PluginContext API shape consistently and guards against concurrent builds.
New code follows standard TS naming conventions; only cache-versioned data format (.ssg-cache.json) added, not new global state.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-engineered incremental-build feature with real design tradeoffs (core-embedded cache, single O(site) manifest, +24 cognitive complexity) — the low 0.49 convention score is a discrepancy driven by pre-existing violations (config.ts is not even in this diff) and generic PascalCase/UPPER_CASE/snake_case rules, while the added code itself is clean. VERDICT: better.

compounding_issues: The seed codebase (a 200-line auth API) is completely discarded by Session 1's greenfield build — zero reuse, but the session was designed as greenfield so the cost is intended
Session 3's dev server was written against the monolithic `buildSite` API and required a 171-line rewrite in Session 4 to participate in the plugin pipeline — early integration work had to be redone

Incremental caching in Session 5 keys invalidation only on source + template hashes, so plugin-config or partial changes outside `templatesDir` won't invalidate cached pages; plugin `onFile` hooks are also skipped for cached pages, meaning plugin side-effects don't re-run on unchanged sources
key_decisions: Session 1: adopt marked + gray-matter as the parsing stack with recursive markdown crawl, HTML escaping, and deterministic date-descending page sort
Session 2: commit to Handlebars as the single template engine with template/layout/partial resolution and path-traversal guards on template names
Session 3: build the live-reload dev server on chokidar + ws with a serialized rebuild queue, port validation, and MIME type mapping

Session 4: introduce the Plugin interface with lifecycle hooks (onStart/beforeBuild/onFile/afterBuild/onEnd), an ssg.config.ts loader, and convert the entire pipeline — including the dev server — to run through plugins
Session 5: add SHA-256 hash-based incremental caching via .ssg-cache.json with template-hash invalidation, stale-output cleanup, and BuildStats surfaced through the CLI
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across all five sessions. Session 1 produced a clean, well-tested single-module SSG; Session 2 extended it with Handlebars templating and security-conscious tests (escaping, missing-template errors); Session 3 added a defensive dev server with path-traversal protection, 405 handling, and live reload; Session 4 was the biggest leap — a genuine architectural refactor into a plugin system with a config loader, preserving all behavior while restructuring the server into a pipeline plugin; Session 5 layered incremental caching and build statistics onto the refactored engine without breaking tests (4/4 passing). Every session exited cleanly, test coverage grew from one 30-line file to four suites, and defensive patterns (escaping, path guards, error handling) were maintained throughout, with complexity growth offset by increasing modularity.
story_review.summary: A textbook progression from greenfield build through feature addition, integration, structural refactor, and cross-cutting optimization, where the plugin architecture from Session 4 directly enabled Session 5's incremental caching — resulting in a coherent, high-quality, monotonically improving codebase.
